create_user.description: Ask the bridge for a whitelist username while the physical link button is pressed. This is the whole pairing flow — no account, no cloud, no expiry. Poll it: the same request answers error type 101 until the button is pressed and success afterwards, so a client sends it every couple of seconds through the ~30 s window rather than trying to detect the press any other way.
create_user.example_notes: Rendered with devicetype "opengreeniot#hub". Arguments render as compact JSON in declared order; generateclientkey is a literal this command has already decided, exactly as an on command's on:true is.
create_user.notes: Answers 200 OK either way — the v1 API wraps outcomes in a JSON array envelope, error type 101 ("link button not pressed") until the button is pressed and success with the credentials after. 101 is the keep-waiting signal, not a failure. Both envelopes are verbatim on the Create User endpoint entry below.

devicetype.description: Client identifier the whitelist entry is filed under, spelled "application#instance" (e.g. "opengreeniot#hub"). The bridge stores it verbatim in its whitelist, so make it say who you are; community documentation bounds the halves at roughly 20 and 19 characters.

returns.description: The credential every later request path embeds. Issued once; store it keyed by bridgeid — the IP is a DHCP lease, the bridgeid is the device — and it keeps working until its whitelist entry is deleted or the bridge is factory reset.
returns.name: username

returns.description: 16-byte hex PSK for the DTLS Entertainment streaming channel. Only obtainable at creation time — which is why generateclientkey is sent unconditionally — so store it beside the username even though nothing in this spec drives Entertainment yet.
returns.name: clientkey

light_set_brightness.description: Set one light's brightness, switching it on in the same write.
light_set_brightness.example_notes: Rendered with bri=200. bri is declared an integer, so it renders as a JSON number, never a quoted string — a renderer substitutes by the declared parameter type. on:true rides along deliberately: a bare bri sent to a light that is off answers error type 201 ("parameter, bri, is not modifiable. Device is set to off."), so the one write carries both.

bri.description: Brightness the light holds while on, 1–254. NOT 0–255: 0 is not "off" (off is the on flag), and 255 is out of range. A consumer mapping a percentage slider should round into this range rather than trust its ends.

light_turn_off.description: Switch one light behind the bridge off.

light_turn_on.description: Switch one light behind the bridge on.
light_turn_on.notes: The reply acknowledges the request rather than reporting resulting state — read the Lights endpoint back after any write. The "on" key is quoted because unquoted `on` is a boolean in YAML 1.1, and this file is read by YAML 1.1 parsers; the wire spelling is the three bare characters.

id.description: Which light, from the enumeration the Hue Light entity's state_command returns. The ids are the bridge's own ("1", "2", …), stable across reboots but not across a factory reset.

username.description: The stored pairing credential; see create_user. No default, deliberately: an unpaired client must fail this send visibly rather than issue a request the bridge answers with error type 1 (unauthorized user).

mac_prefixes.notes: Philips Lighting BV's own block, carried by the BSB001/BSB002 bridges (see the live probe under `examples` below). Not subdivided and not a chip vendor's, so an address in it really is Philips hardware -- but Philips put it on lamps, switches and sensors too, so it means "something Philips made", not "a bridge".
Signify B.V., seen on the 2025 Bridge Pro (BSB003). Same caveat: the block is the company's whole output, not this product.

device.name: Philips Hue Bridge
device.notes:
Hue Bridge v2 exposes a local HTTP REST API on port 80. GET /api/config returns bridge metadata without authentication. Control endpoints require a whitelist username created by POST /api while the physical link button is pressed. Discovery should prefer the Hue-specific mDNS service and fall back to UPnP/SSDP device description XML.
HTTPS / CLIP V2: current firmware also serves HTTPS on port 443 (the _hue._tcp mDNS SRV record advertises 443; proper CA-issued certificates since fw 1971060010). CLIP API v2 runs there: resources under /clip/v2/resource/* with header "hue-application-key: <username>" (the same POST /api pairing issues the key; generateclientkey:true adds an entertainment clientkey), plus a server-sent event stream at /eventstream/clip/v2 (HTTPS-only). Signify has announced plain-HTTP retirement on the gen-2 bridge in a future firmware update — new clients should target HTTPS + CLIP v2.
TLS: the HTTPS certificate is a per-device leaf whose subject CN is the 16-hex-char bridgeid in lowercase, issued by Signify's private bridge root CA (issuer CN "root-bridge") — deliberately not a public chain, so stock certificate verification fails on every Hue bridge and a client must verify the Hue way instead: check the leaf CN equals the bridgeid it expects (learned from mDNS TXT or GET /api/config), then pin that leaf keyed by bridgeid — trust on first use. A later pin mismatch is a different device or an interception, never a rotation to accept silently; do not fall back to plain HTTP on a pin failure. The Bridge Pro (BSB003) is HTTPS-only, so this verification path is the only way to reach it at all.
N-UPNP DISCOVERY: https://discovery.meethue.com/ (no auth) returns internalipaddress, id, and port (443) of registered bridges — a third documented discovery method alongside mDNS and SSDP.
HUE BRIDGE PRO (BSB003, Sept 2025): HTTPS-only (no port 80 at all) and no UPnP/SSDP — mDNS is the only local discovery; new MAC prefix C42996. This spec's SSDP method and HTTP/80 assumptions are BSB002-only.
SECURITY: CVE-2020-6007 (Check Point, 2020) — heap overflow on long Zigbee ZCL string during commissioning, RCE on bridge fw ≤ 1935144020, patched in 1935144040. Pwn2Own Cork 2025: CVE-2026-3555 — Zigbee→bridge heap-overflow RCE in the ipbridge "Download Blob" FSM (Synacktiv); the patched family CVE-2026-3555…3562 also covers signature-verification bypass and HomeKit hk_hap auth bypass (TCP 8080). Keep bridges on current firmware.
FIRMWARE: public no-auth update API — GET https://firmware.meethue.com/v1/checkupdate?deviceTypeId=BSB002&version=<swversion> returns binaryUrl, fileSize, md5, and release notes (latest as of 2026-07-31: 1978074000, "1.78_SR2"). Binaries are signed/encrypted .fw2 containers; an md5-verified BSB002 1978074000 image is archived in the verification research dir (research/hue-bridge/firmware/).

issued_to_client: API username (bearer-equivalent; sent in the URL path on plain HTTP)
Entertainment clientkey (16-byte DTLS PSK, hex) — only obtainable at create time, so create_user always asks for it
credentials.notes: The username is transmitted in the URL on unencrypted HTTP and never expires on its own. Treat it as a long-lived LAN secret and delete unused whitelist entries. CLIP v2 sends the same credential in the hue-application-key header over HTTPS, keeping it out of URLs.
stored_on_device: Whitelist usernames issued to paired clients
ZigBee network key for paired lights

factory_reset.effect: Clears every whitelist username and the bridge's own ZigBee network configuration. Paired bulbs stay joined to the old, now-forgotten network and must be re-added (or reset themselves) afterwards, so a bridge reset is a much bigger event than a WiFi device reset.

procedures.indicator: LEDs cycle and the bridge reboots.
procedures.name: Recessed restore button

steps.action: Press the recessed button on the underside of the bridge with a paperclip and hold until the LEDs cycle.
Wait for the bridge to reboot and re-acquire a DHCP lease.

methods.description: Plug the bridge into the router with Ethernet and power it. It takes a DHCP lease and starts answering mDNS/SSDP; there is no WiFi passphrase to transfer, so there is no setup AP and no credential encryption problem.

steps.action: Connect the bridge to the LAN over Ethernet and apply power.
steps.expect: All three front LEDs light; the bridge answers _hue._tcp.local.

methods.description: The bridge issues an API username (whitelist entry) to any client that asks within roughly 30 seconds of the physical link button being pressed. This is a proximity proof, not an account: no cloud login is involved and the username keeps working after the vendor cloud goes away. commands.create_user is this flow as an executable command — poll it every couple of seconds; error type 101 means keep waiting, not failure.

clientkey.notes: Entertainment DTLS PSK, issued only at create time — a re-pair without generateclientkey never sees it again, which is why create_user sends it unconditionally.

username.notes: The value every later request's `credential:username` parameter names. Store it keyed by bridgeid, not IP.

steps.action: POST /api with a devicetype string to confirm the bridge rejects unauthorized clients.
steps.expect: Error type 101, 'link button not pressed' — proves the bridge is reachable and unpaired.

steps.action: Press the round link button on the top of the bridge.
Repeat POST /api within the pairing window.
steps.expect: success.username — store it; it is the only credential needed for all later control.

setup.notes: Two separate things have to happen before a client can control a Hue Bridge: the bridge has to reach the LAN (Ethernet only — the v2 bridge has no WiFi radio and no credential provisioning of its own), and the client has to be authorized by the physical link button. Only the second step is a protocol flow.

rejoin.notes: Moving the bridge to a different router is a cable move plus a new DHCP lease. Stored usernames survive, so previously authorized clients keep working; only the IP changes, which is why clients must key off the TXT bridgeid rather than the address.

testing.notes: Driven live 2026-08-14 against a real BSB002 bridge (bridgeid 001788FFFEAABBCC, apiversion 1.78.0, swversion 1978074000), discovered via _hue._tcp mDNS whose TXT bridgeid matched GET /api/config exactly. Executed as documented: GET /api/config unauthenticated returns the whitelist-free config object on BOTH http:80 and https:443 (same body); POST /api with a devicetype and no button press returned the error envelope byte-identical to this spec's example — [{"error":{"type":101, "address":"","description":"link button not pressed"}}]; GET /clip/v2/resource without (or with a bogus) hue-application-key answers 403 with an HTML body, confirming the CLIP v2 key gate. Halted at the physical link button (nobody home to press it): username creation, light control and the eventstream remain unexercised by us.

entities.name: Hue Light
entities.notes: One entity, stamped out per light. The Lights endpoint answers a JSON object keyed by light id, so enumeration and every child's state ride one GET — poll that, never the lights one at a time, and re-read it after any write because a PUT's reply is an acknowledgement, not state. Brightness is 1–254 (see light_set_brightness). state.reachable is worth honouring when rendering: a bulb powered off at the wall keeps its last state here with reachable false, and a toggle drawn live for it is a lie. Color and color temperature are deliberately not bound yet — a set_color role needs multi-value parameters (xy or ct plus colormode) that no consumer resolves today; the state fields are documented on Set Light State for when one does.

entities.name: Hue Sensor
entities.notes: Declarative, unlike the light above. The Sensors endpoint enumerates motion, temperature, light-level and switch sensors the same instanced way Lights does, but the population is heterogeneous — each sensor type carries a different state shape — so binding them properly is a worked pass of its own (instances plus a per-type mapping), not a guessed mapping here.

helpful_urls.description: HA core integration over the local Hue bridge API v2 (CLIP); where this protocol runs in production.
helpful_urls.title: Home Assistant Philips Hue integration

http_endpoints.description: Unauthenticated bridge identity: name, bridgeid, MAC, modelid, API and software versions. This is the short form the bridge answers without a username (the full config — whitelist, network settings — lives at /api/{username}/config); it is how a client learns the bridgeid when discovery could not say (SSDP finds the bridge, but only mDNS TXT carries bridgeid), and the bridgeid is also what the HTTPS certificate's CN must equal — see the TLS paragraph in device.notes.
http_endpoints.name: Bridge Config

fields.description: 16-hex-char bridge identity, uppercase: the MAC with FFFE spliced into the middle (EUI-64). The stable key everything else — credentials, TLS pins, scan identity — is filed under.
fields.name: bridgeid

fields.description: BSB001 (v1 round), BSB002 (v2 square), BSB003 (2025 Bridge Pro).
fields.name: modelid

fields.description: User-assigned bridge name; defaults to 'Philips hue'.
fields.name: name

http_endpoints.description: Press-link pairing endpoint that creates a whitelist username when the bridge link button has been pressed. HTTP status is 200 either way; outcomes ride the v1 array envelope (payload_formats.V1Envelope, whose example is this endpoint's pre-press reply verbatim). Error type 101 is the keep-polling signal, not a failure; after the button, the success envelope in the example below. commands.create_user is the executable form of this call.
http_endpoints.name: Create User

fields.description: Application identifier used for the created Hue whitelist username, spelled application#instance.
fields.name: devicetype

fields.description: Ask for the Entertainment DTLS PSK alongside the username. Only honoured at creation time — a username created without it can never get one — so always send true.
fields.name: generateclientkey

fields.description: Whitelist credential, ~40 URL-safe characters; every authenticated v1 path embeds it.
fields.name: username

fields.description: 32 hex chars — the 16-byte Entertainment PSK. Present only when generateclientkey was sent.
fields.name: clientkey

http_endpoints.description: Enumerate Hue lights paired to the bridge. The reply is a JSON object keyed by light id — enumeration and every light's full state in one request, which is exactly what the Hue Light entity's instances block binds. Poll this, never the lights one at a time: community rate-limit guidance is roughly ten light writes a second and far fewer whole-bridge reads. Real replies carry more keys per light than the example (capabilities, config, swupdate); the example is the load-bearing subset, with one color light that is on and one dimmable light that is off.
http_endpoints.name: Lights

http_endpoints.description: Set on/off, brightness, color, color temperature, effects, or alert state for a light. The reply acknowledges each changed attribute (see the example) rather than reporting resulting state, so a client reads Lights back after writing. Sending bri (or any modifiable attribute) to a light that is off answers error type 201 — carry "on": true in the same write, as light_set_brightness does.
http_endpoints.name: Set Light State

fields.description: Relay state. The only attribute writable while the light is off.
fields.name: on

fields.description: Brightness held while on; see commands.light_set_brightness.
fields.name: bri

fields.description: Hue angle scaled to 16 bits (65535 ≈ 360°). Color lights only.
fields.name: hue

fields.description: Saturation, 0 white to 254 full color. Color lights only.
fields.name: sat

fields.description: CIE 1931 [x, y] point, each 0.0–1.0. The colormode color apps usually drive.
fields.name: xy

fields.description: Color temperature in mireds: 153 ≈ 6500 K cold, 500 = 2000 K warm.
fields.name: ct

fields.description: Fade duration in deciseconds; the bridge defaults to 4 (400 ms) when absent.
fields.name: transitiontime

http_endpoints.description: Enumerate Hue sensors exposed by the bridge.
http_endpoints.name: Sensors

http_endpoints.description: Enumerate rooms, zones, and light groups.
http_endpoints.name: Groups

http_endpoints.description: CLIP API v2 resource tree (devices, lights, rooms, scenes, …) over HTTPS/443. Requires header 'hue-application-key: <username>'; the same POST /api pairing issues the key (generateclientkey:true adds an entertainment clientkey).
http_endpoints.name: CLIP v2 Resources

http_endpoints.description: Server-sent event stream for CLIP v2 state changes. HTTPS-only, same hue-application-key header.
http_endpoints.name: CLIP v2 Event Stream

V1Envelope.description: The CLIP v1 outcome envelope. Every v1 write and the pairing call answer HTTP 200 with a JSON ARRAY of outcome objects — one element per attribute touched, each either a success or an error — never a bare object. The HTTP status code says nothing; a client reads outcomes from the envelope.
parse_rules: Parse the body as JSON. An array is an outcome envelope, one element per attribute or request; a bare object is a successful GET reply.
An element {"success": {…}} acknowledges one attribute write (key = attribute path, value = accepted value); {"error": {…}} carries integer `type`, string `address`, string `description`.
error.type 101 (link button not pressed) is create_user's keep-polling signal, not a failure.
error.type 1 (unauthorized user) means the stored username no longer exists on the bridge — surface re-pairing; retrying cannot succeed.
error.type 201 (parameter not modifiable) is the answer to writing bri while the light is off — carry "on": true in the same write, as light_set_brightness does.
A mixed envelope is possible: a write touching two attributes can succeed on one and error on the other, so check every element.
